title: Vertical giants and rare boss clouds
teaches: How a cumulus becomes a thunderstorm, counting the thunder, and the rare clouds to stay up for

blocks.text: Think back to the cumulus in the first lesson. A thermal rises, reaches its dew point and turns to cloud, and then, because condensing vapour gives back heat, its cloudy air cools only about 5 °C per kilometre as it climbs. As long as the air around it cools faster than that, the cloud stays warmer than its neighbours and keeps growing. So the real question about any heap is not whether it can rise, but where it will stop.

Three things decide that. The **sun** sets how warm the thermals start. The **moisture** sets the cloud base, and so how soon the cloud gets the extra heat from condensing. And an [[inversion|env]] overhead can stop the cloud dead, just as it flattened the stratocumulus in the second lesson. A heap that runs into warm air above it is suddenly colder than its surroundings, and it can climb no further.

Forecasters name heaps by how far they got. **Humilis** is small and flat, wider than it is tall: fair weather. **Mediocris** is about as tall as it is wide. **Congestus** towers, with hard, bright cauliflower tops, and it is the one to watch, because on an unstable day it may keep going.

This figure is the chart glider pilots and forecasters use for exactly this question. Twice a day, weather stations release balloons carrying a small radio with a thermometer and a moisture sensor, which reports the temperature and dew point every few seconds as the balloon climbs. The solid violet line is that report: the temperature of the air around the cloud at each height. (The dashed violet line is the same air at dawn, before the sun warmed the ground.) The teal line is the dew point. The orange line is the rising bubble: 10 °C per kilometre while it is clear air, then about 5 inside the cloud. Temperature runs left to right, warmer to the right. Wherever orange lies to the right of violet, the bubble is warmer than its neighbours and keeps rising. Where the two lines cross, it stops.

blocks.caption: A summer day over farm country, with a warm layer a couple of kilometres up.
blocks.task: Grow a cumulus congestus: a tower several kilometres tall.

blocks.text: If nothing stops the tower, how high can it go? About 10 to 12 kilometres. All the way up through the weather, the air gets colder with height, because it is warmed from below, by the ground. But at around that height it stops cooling, and higher still it actually grows warmer. The reason is a gas called **ozone**, a rarer form of oxygen whose molecules have three atoms instead of the usual two. Up there, the sun’s harshest ultraviolet light splits ordinary oxygen molecules apart, and the loose atoms join other molecules to make ozone, so the high air holds a thin layer of it. Ozone in turn soaks up more ultraviolet light, which warms the air around it: a second heater, this time from above. (It is the same layer that shields your skin from the worst of the sunburn.) The boundary between the two is called the **tropopause**, and above it lies the **stratosphere**. It is one enormous, permanent inversion, and it is what this course has been calling the top of the weather. Even the most violent tower cannot climb far into it.

So a tower that reaches the tropopause hits a ceiling. Air keeps pouring up from below, and it has to go somewhere, so like a fountain hitting a ceiling it spreads out sideways. The top, long since frozen to ice, fans out into a flat, wide **anvil**, often blown far downwind by the strong winds up there, which usually means out ahead of the storm, since the storm drifts the same way. A heap that has grown that tall, with an icy top and rain falling from its base, is a **cumulonimbus**: the thunderstorm. The anvil is the surest sign; the rain comes with it.

In the next figure you also control how fast the air around cools with height. Remember the test: inside the cloud the bubble cools about 5 °C per kilometre, so the faster the surrounding air cools beyond that, the bigger the bubble’s lead in temperature grows and the higher it goes.

blocks.caption: The same day, with the instability control added.
blocks.task: Remove the lid and make the air unstable enough to grow a cumulonimbus.

blocks.text: A single storm cell lives for about an hour. Watch one through its life.

blocks.caption: One thunderstorm cell, from first heap to last shower.
blocks.task: Run the storm to the end of its life.

blocks.text: In the **growing stage** the tower is all updraught, rising air feeding the cloud from below. In the **mature stage**, rain and hail have grown heavy enough to fall through the updraught. **Hail** is ice that grew in the storm’s strongest updraughts, A small ice pellet falls until it meets an updraught strong enough to blow it back up, and the updraughts in a big storm are uneven, gusting stronger and weaker, so a stone can be tossed up and dropped many times. Each trip through the supercooled water freezes on a new layer, until it is too heavy for any updraught to hold up, and it falls out as hail. As the rain and hail fall they drag air down with them, and some of the rain evaporates, which chills that air; cold air is heavy, so it sinks faster still: the storm now has an updraught and a downdraught side by side, and this is when it brings lightning, downpours and sudden gusts. In the **dissipating stage** the cold downdraught spreads out along the ground, cuts off the warm air that fed the updraught, and the cloud rains itself out, leaving its anvil drifting away downwind.

Inside the tower, soft hail, ice crystals and supercooled droplets are colliding all the time. All matter is made of atoms, and every atom has tiny negatively charged particles, **electrons**, around its outside. When two things rub or bump, a few electrons can be scraped from one onto the other, so one ends up negative and the other positive: that is why a balloon rubbed on your hair sticks to the wall. Scientists are still working out exactly what decides which way the electrons go in a cloud, but in the middle of a storm each collision tends to leave the small crystal a little positive and the heavier hail a little negative. The updraught carries the light crystals to the top of the storm while the heavy hail sinks lower, so the cloud separates into charged regions, like a gigantic battery. Opposite charges attract. When the separated charge grows large enough, its pull on the electrons in the air between becomes so strong that it tears them off their molecules. Air with loose electrons in it conducts electricity, like a wire, so a narrow path opens up, and the charge rushes through it in a spark kilometres long: **lightning**.

The spark heats the air along its path to about 30,000 °C in a few millionths of a second, five times hotter than the surface of the sun. The air expands so suddenly that it sends out a shock wave, and we hear it as **thunder**.

You see the flash almost at once, because light covers the distance in a tiny fraction of a second. Sound is slow by comparison, about **343 metres a second**, so it takes about **three seconds to cover a kilometre**. Count the seconds from flash to thunder and divide by three to get the distance in kilometres. (The figure runs fast to save waiting, but it counts the real seconds you would hear.)

blocks.caption: A storm somewhere off over the hills.
blocks.task: Make the storm strike, and count.

blocks.text: Lightning doesn’t always come down under the storm. The positive charge sits up in the anvil, which spreads many kilometres ahead of the storm, and a bolt from it can run sideways under clear blue sky and come down ten kilometres away. People call it a bolt from the blue.

The safety rule follows from this: if you can count less than thirty seconds, the storm is within ten kilometres, close enough to be hit. Get indoors, or at least off high, open ground, and stay there until thirty minutes after the last thunder. A dying storm can still throw a late bolt, and the half hour is how long it takes to be sure it has really gone.
The last few clouds are rare. You might watch a whole summer before seeing one, and when you do, call it in: it goes in your journal.

When a strong, steady wind blows across a mountain ridge, the air is pushed up the windward side and then, in stable air, it overshoots on the far side. It sinks too far, and it is the first lesson’s test run backwards. In stable air, the surroundings cool by less than 10 °C per kilometre as you go up, so going *down* they warm by less than 10 °C per kilometre. The sinking air warms by the full 10 °C, as all sinking clear air does, so it ends up warmer and lighter than its new neighbours, and rises again. It goes on bobbing up and down downwind of the ridge: the nudged parcel from the first lesson, swinging back and forth in a valley. These **standing waves** stay in place, like the ripples downstream of a rock in a river, while the wind blows through them. Where the air rises through the crest of a wave it cools, and if it is moist enough it reaches its dew point and a cloud forms there.

blocks.caption: Wind blowing over a mountain ridge.
blocks.task: Get the wind and moisture right to make a lens cloud.

blocks.text: The result is a **lenticularis**, Latin for lens-shaped, usually an altocumulus, since the crests that hold a cloud are mostly a few kilometres up on the middle floor. Unlike the lumpy altocumulus of the third lesson, it is smooth, because it is one crest of one wave, not a churning layer: a smooth lens, or flying saucer, that sits still beside the mountain even in a gale. Air enters its upwind edge, rises and turns to cloud; it leaves the downwind edge, sinks, warms back above its dew point, and the droplets evaporate. The cloud stays put while the air races through it.

Under the anvil of a strong thunderstorm, the sky sometimes fills with smooth, rounded pouches hanging downward. Air laden with ice and droplets sinks out of the anvil’s base. It does warm as it sinks, like any sinking air, but this air is full of ice and droplets, and as it sinks into drier air they evaporate, and evaporating takes up heat. That takes away most of the warming, so the air warms only about 5 °C per kilometre, the cloudy rate from the first lesson run backwards, while the surrounding air, going down, warms faster than that, about 6 or 7 °C per kilometre on a typical day. So the sinking air stays cooler than its surroundings and keeps sinking, in rounded lobes: an upside-down heap, just as a cloudy bubble keeps rising because condensing water warms it.

blocks.caption: The underside of an anvil, late in a storm.
blocks.task: Let the cold air sink until pouches form.

blocks.text: These are **mammatus**. They look alarming, and they do mean a vigorous storm is near, but the pouches themselves are harmless. Since the anvil streams out ahead of the storm and lingers after it, they are most often seen as the storm moves away, once the worst has passed.

Last, the rarest and shortest-lived of all. Where a layer of fast air slides over a layer of slow air (wind shear again, as with the cirrus hooks), the boundary between them ripples, just as wind ripples a pond. Each ripple’s crest pokes up into the fast air, which shoves it forward, while its trough dips into the slow air, which holds it back. Stable air tries to flatten the ripple; the shear tries to tip it over. If the difference in speed is great enough, the shear wins, and each crest is pushed further forward than its base until it curls over like breaking surf.

blocks.caption: A cloud layer with fast air above and slower air below.
blocks.task: Increase the difference in wind until the waves curl over.

blocks.text: These are **Kelvin-Helmholtz waves**, called *fluctus* in the International Cloud Atlas, the world’s official book of cloud names. They last only a minute or two before the curls mix themselves away, so anyone who sees them is lucky. To pilots they mean turbulence.
The final check. First name each cloud in the photos, then read what a few changing skies are up to.

blocks.caption: The sky over a few hours. What is it up to?

items.question: Heaps were still growing tall at midday on a hot, sticky day. What’s up by mid-afternoon?
items.why: Cumulus still towering by midday on an unstable day can grow into cumulonimbus by afternoon: lightning, downpours and gusts.

items.question: The balloon report shows a strong warm layer two kilometres up. What will today’s heaps do?
options: Flatten out under it: fair weather
items.why: A heap that runs into warmer air above it is colder than its surroundings and stops there.

items.question: Flash, then thunder 12 seconds later. How far is the strike?
items.why: 12 ÷ 3 is 4 km. Well within reach: get indoors.

items.question: The storm has gone quiet. The last thunder was ten minutes ago. Is it safe to go back outside?
options: Not yet: wait thirty minutes after the last thunder
Only if the sky overhead is blue
items.why: A dying storm can throw a late bolt, even out of blue sky. Wait thirty minutes after the last thunder.

items.question: A smooth lens of cloud sits beside the peak all afternoon in a strong wind, never moving. What is it?
options: A lens cloud in a mountain wave
items.why: Wind over the ridge bobs up and down in standing waves; the cloud forms in a crest and stays put while the air races through. It goes in the journal.

items.question: At dawn, little turrets sprout from a layer of altocumulus. What should you expect?
items.why: Turreted altocumulus, castellanus, means the middle sky is unstable: a classic warning of afternoon storms.

learned: A heap grows until it is no longer warmer than the air around it; an inversion can stop it, and forecasters name it by height: humilis, mediocris, congestus.
The tropopause, 10 to 12 km up, is a permanent inversion: a tower that reaches it spreads into an anvil, and a heap that tall and rainy is a cumulonimbus.
A storm cell lives about an hour: updraught, then updraught and downdraught together, then the downdraught smothers it.
Count from flash to thunder and divide by three for the distance in kilometres. Under thirty seconds, get indoors.
Rare clouds: lens clouds in mountain waves, mammatus under anvils, and Kelvin-Helmholtz waves where fast air slides over slow.

cumulonimbus.title: Cumulonimbus
cumulonimbus.text: A heap that grew to the tropopause, 10 to 12 km up, and spread into an ice anvil. Grows, matures and rains out in about an hour, with lightning, downpours, hail and gusts.

lightning.title: Counting the thunder
lightning.text: Colliding hail and ice crystals separate charge inside a storm until it sparks: lightning, heating the air to about 30,000 °C, which bangs into thunder. Sound travels about a kilometre every three seconds. Count from flash to thunder and divide by three for kilometres. Under thirty seconds, you are within reach: get indoors.

lenticularis.title: Lens cloud (lenticularis)
lenticularis.text: A smooth lens parked in a standing wave downwind of a mountain. Air turns to cloud as it rises into the crest and evaporates as it leaves; the cloud stays put while the wind blows through it.

mammatus.title: Mammatus
mammatus.text: Smooth pouches hanging under a thunderstorm anvil, where cold, laden air sinks out of it, kept cold by its own evaporating ice and droplets. A sign of a vigorous storm nearby, though the pouches themselves are harmless.

fluctus.title: Kelvin-Helmholtz waves (fluctus)
fluctus.text: Breaking-surf curls on top of a cloud layer, where fast air slides over slow. They last a minute or two. To pilots they mean turbulence.
